newsitem.title: USA: Lebanese leader in U.S. for aid to Beirut meeting.
newsitem.headline: Lebanese leader in U.S. for aid to Beirut meeting.

text.p: Lebanese Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri arrived on Sunday for a U.S.-sponsored international meeting on aid to Beirut amid a new flurry of violence between Israel and Lebanon.
Hariri's plane landed at Andrews Air Force Base in nearby Maryland, a U.S. military spokeswoman said.
On the eve of the talks on Monday, Israeli planes fired rockets at suspected guerrilla targets in southeast Lebanon.

The raids followed a clash in the zone on Saturday in which an Israeli brigadier was slightly injured and two Moslem guerrillas were killed. On Friday, Israel said Katyusha rockets fired from Lebanon hit northern Israel.
The weekend violence on the last active Arab-Israeli battlefront came as potential donors gathered for the "Friends of Lebanon" conference at the State Department.
Hariri has said he would ask some 30 countries and international institutions invited to the one-day session for contributions of up to $5 billion for reconstruction projects in the next five years.

Officials said Lebanon deserved political support and financial help after making a huge effort in the past four years to rebuild and restore economic, political, social and security stability following 16 years of civil war.
The State Department expects "important announcements" to be made at the meeting, but has given no details.

"I think you should treat this as a serious event, an event ... that will have a lot of interest in terms of some of the announcements we'll be making," spokesman Nicholas Burns told reporters on Friday.
Asked about the U.S. travel ban on Lebanon, which Beirut has pressed Washington to lift, Burns called it "a very complicated, complex issue."

"I don't want to anticipate what decisions may or may not be made on it, but it's certainly an issue that I think Prime Minister Hariri will bring to the table on Monday ... and we'll be prepared to discuss it with him," he added.

Washington insists its ban on U.S. citizens travelling to Lebanon is a purely security matter dating back to the seizure of American hostages by pro-Iranian groups there in the 1980s. But Beirut suspects it is being used as a lever to force it into signing a peace treaty with Israel.
